Finding Square Roots

You're going to find the square root of any number — without using any built-in function. All you need is multiplication, a bit of guessing, and a clever trick that cuts your search in half every time.

Along the way, you'll pick up Python basics: expressions, variables, if-else, loops, and functions — all by solving one real problem.

Part 1: Squares and Square Roots

Open a Jupyter notebook or Google Colab. You can type a math expression into a cell and press Shift+Enter to run it — Python will be your calculator.

What Is a Square?

The square of a number is the number multiplied by itself.

What is the square of 2? Type 2 * 2 into a cell and press Shift+Enter.

More Squares

What is the square of 3? Of 4? Of 5? Compute each one in Python.

Going Backwards — Square Roots

The square root is the reverse question: what number, multiplied by itself, gives you the target?

What is the square root of 16? Of 25? Of 9?

Check each answer by squaring it in Python.

A Harder Question

What is the square root of 5?

It's not a whole number. But you know something about it already.

Is the square root of 5 between 2 and 3? How do you know?

Can you take a guess? Don't overthink it — just pick a number between 2 and 3.

Part 2: The Guessing Game

You know sqrt(5) is between 2 and 3. Let's find it by guessing, checking, and narrowing down.

Check Your Guess

Pick a number between 2 and 3 as your guess for sqrt(5). Square it in Python. Was it too high or too low?

Take a Better Guess

Based on your first guess, you now have a narrower range. Take a new guess inside that range and check again. Is your new guess too high or too low?

Repeat this one more time — three guesses total.

Use Variables to Track the Range

Instead of keeping track of the range in your head, use two variables: lo (the lower bound) and hi (the upper bound). Compute your guess as the midpoint: guess = (lo + hi) / 2.

Run the code below, then update lo or hi by hand and run it again.

Let Python Decide

You've been deciding manually: "too high → update hi, too low → update lo." Python can make this decision for you using if and else.

Run the code below. Then run the block from guess = ... to the last print(...) a few more times. Watch lo and hi get closer together!

Each guess cuts your search range in half. After the first guess, you have half the range. After the second, a quarter. After ten guesses, you've narrowed it down to $\frac{1}{1024}$ of the original range.

This "halving" strategy is called binary search — "binary" because you split the range in two each time.

Part 3: Let the Loop Do the Work

Copying and pasting the same block over and over is tedious. Python's for loop can repeat it for you — as many times as you want.

20 Guesses in One Go

Put your guess-and-update logic inside a for loop that runs 20 times. Does your guess get closer to the real answer?

Check Your Answer!

Python has a built-in square root function. Let's see if your answer matches.

Try Another Number

Now find the square root of 10 using the same approach.

What should lo and hi start at?

Part 4: Build Your Own Square Root Function

You've found sqrt(5) and sqrt(10) by repeating the same code with different numbers. What if you want sqrt(15)? Or sqrt(1000)? Copying the code each time is messy.

A function lets you package code so you can call it with any input.

Write mysqrt

Fill in the two missing lines. When the guess is too high, which bound should change? When it's too low?

Test Your Function

Test mysqrt with several numbers and compare with math.sqrt.

Try mysqrt(15, 3, 4, 20) first — does it match?

Congratulations! In one sitting you learned:

  • Python as a calculator — expressions like 2 * 2
  • Variables — lo, hi, guess to track your state
  • Conditional logic — if / else to make decisions
  • Loops — for to repeat work automatically
  • Functions — def to package reusable logic
  • Binary search — the algorithm that finds answers by halving the search space

This "halving" strategy doesn't just work for square roots. It works for cube roots, logarithms, and searching through sorted lists. It's one of the most important algorithms in computer science — and you just invented it.

Summary

Step What you did Python concept learned
1 Computed squares (2×2, 3×3, ...) Expressions
2 Reversed the question (sqrt of 16, 25, 9) Thinking backwards
3 Guessed sqrt(5), checked by squaring Variables (guess)
4 Tracked the range with lo and hi Variables (lo, hi)
5 Automated the high/low decision if / else
6 Repeated the guessing 20 times for loop
7 Packaged it as mysqrt(num, lo, hi, iterations) Functions (def)

You started by typing 2 * 2 into Python. You ended with a function that computes square roots to arbitrary precision using binary search. Every step was something you could reason about — no magic, no memorization.

Going further:

  • Cube roots: The same halving trick works — just check guess * guess * guess instead of guess * guess. Try writing mycuberoot(num, lo, hi, iterations).
  • More precision: Instead of a fixed number of iterations, stop when abs(guess * guess - num) is smaller than some tiny number like 0.0000001.
  • The full Binary Search chapter on this site applies the same idea to nth roots, logarithms, and searching sorted arrays.
